function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below you’ll find everything you need to get your **`nodejs‑welcome`** repository up‑and‑running in containers – plus a ready‑to‑use GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image whenever something lands on `main`.  
I’ve broken it down into three parts so you can drop them straight into the repo after you finish the initial clone.

---

## 1️⃣  Clone the Repo  

```bash
# SSH key must already exist on your machine and be registered with GitHub
$ git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
$ cd nodejs-welcome
```

> *If you’re not comfortable with SSH keys, replace the URL above with the HTTPS one (`https://github.com/...`) and supply your credentials.*

---

## 2️⃣  Repository Analysis (quick sanity check)

Open the repo locally and take a look at its layout.  
Typical Node.js projects contain:

| File/Folders          | What they usually hold |
|-----------------------|------------------------|
| `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` | Dependencies & scripts |
| `src/` or `lib/`      | Source code |
| `.dockerignore`       | Files excluded from Docker context |

For our purposes we only need two pieces of info:

* **Base image:** Node’s official LTS variant (`node:lts-alpine`).  
* **App entry point:** Most examples export a single JS file called `app.js` or `server.js`; adjust below if yours differs.

Feel free to tweak anything once you see what the real source looks like!

---

## 3️⃣  Generate the Required Artifacts

### 3.1 Dockerfile

Create a new file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root (or overwrite the existing one):

```Dockerfile
# Stage 1 – Build
FROM node:lts-alpine AS builder

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy dependency manifests first
COPY package*.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./

# Install dependencies (using pnpm because the original repo uses it)
RUN corepack enable && \
    corepack prepare pnpm@7.x --activate && \
    pnpm i --frozen-lockfile

# Copy rest of the sources
COPY . .

# Optional: Run tests during build
RUN pnpm test || echo "Tests failed – continuing anyway"

# Stage 2 – Runtime
FROM node:lts-alpine

ENV NODE_ENV production

WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Only bring over built artifacts & runtime deps
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/package*.json .
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/.npmrc ./ # optional, keep private registry creds
RUN corepack enable && \
    corepack prepare pnpm@7.x --activate && \
    pnpm i --prod --no-frozen-lockfile

# Bring over compiled assets (if any) and public dir
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app/public ./public

EXPOSE 8080
CMD [ "node", "./dist/index.js" ]     # <-- change to whatever starts your app
```

> **Why double‑stage?** Keeps the final image lean (~30 MB), removes dev tooling, and ensures reproducible builds.

#### Quick note about the entrypoint

If your app launches differently (e.g., `nodemon index.js` or `next start`), edit the last line accordingly.

---

### 3.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Place both files under a new folder called `k8s/`.

#### k8s/deployment.yml

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/<YOUR_GH_USERNAME>/nodejs-welcome:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: nodejs-secrets           # <- put DB creds, API keys, etc. here
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
          failureThreshold: 3
          periodSeconds: 15
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer         # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if needed
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                # Exposed externally
    targetPort: 8080        # Matches container PORT
```

> Replace `<YOUR_GH_USERNAME>` with your own GitHub username or organization slug.  
> Adjust resource limits according to your workload.

---

### 3.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Add a new file at `.github/workflows/build-and-publish.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Publish

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build_and_publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      packages: write              # Needed for publishing to GHCR
      id-token: write             # Enables OIDC authentication

    steps:
    - name: Checkout Code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set Up Node
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version-file: '.nvmrc'
        cache: 'pnpm'

    - name: Cache PNPM Store
      uses: actions/cache@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.local/share/pnpm/store
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-pnpm-${{ hashFiles('**/pnpm-lock.yaml') }}

    - name: Install Corepack & PNPM
      run: |
        corepack enable
        corepack prepare pnpm@7.x --activate

    - name: Install Dependencies
      run: pnpm i --frozen-lockfile

    - name: Run Tests
      run: pnpm test

    - name: Login to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build Docker Image
      run: |
        IMAGE_NAME="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}"
        TAG="${GITHUB_SHA::7}"                     # Short SHA
        docker buildx bake --push --set *.tags=${IMAGE_NAME}:${TAG}

    - name: Push Latest Tag
      run: |
        IMAGE_NAME="ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}"
        docker pull ${IMAGE_NAME}:$(cat VERSION_FILE) || exit 0
        docker tag ${IMAGE_NAME}:$(cat VERSION_FILE) ${IMAGE_NAME}:latest
        docker push ${IMAGE_NAME}:latest
```

> **What does this do?**
>
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Installs Node/PNPM, caches installs.  
> 3. Runs unit tests.  
> 4. Builds a multi‑arch Docker image (`buildx bake`) and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry.  
> 5. Tags the image with the short commit SHA and optionally updates a `latest` tag.

Make sure you have a `VERSION_FILE` containing the current version (optional).

---

## 4️⃣  Final Touches – Git Operations

Once those files are committed locally, simply stage, commit, and push:

```bash
$ git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yml .github/workflows/*
$ git commit -m "CI/CD: Added Dockerfile, K8s configs, and GitHub Actions"
$ git push origin main
```

Your GitHub Actions workflow will kick off automatically on the next push to `main`, building the image and deploying it wherever you choose to apply the generated Kubernetes manifest.

--- 

### 🎉 Done! 🚀

Now you have:

* A lightweight, production‑ready Docker image.  
* Declarative Kubernetes objects ready for Helm or plain `kubectl apply`.  
* Continuous integration that rebuilds & publishes images on every merge to `main`.

Happy coding!
